title: Object-Oriented Programming
tagline: Bundling data with the behaviour that guards it — what classes, inheritance, and polymorphism really buy you, and how JavaScript builds it all on prototypes.

sections.content:
**Object-oriented programming (OOP)** organises a program around **objects**: units that bundle *state* (data) with the *behaviour* (methods) allowed to read and change it. Instead of global data structures manipulated by free-standing procedures, each object owns its data and exposes a small, deliberate interface. Callers ask an object to do something — `account.withdraw(30)` — and the object decides how, enforcing its own rules.

The idea is older than most of the languages that use it. **Simula 67** introduced classes, objects, and inheritance for simulation; **Smalltalk** (Alan Kay and colleagues at Xerox PARC, 1970s) made "everything is an object communicating by messages" the whole language, and Kay coined the term "object-oriented". C++, Objective-C, Java, C#, Python, Ruby, Swift, Kotlin, and TypeScript all brought variations of the model to the mainstream, which is why most production code you will read uses at least some OOP.

OOP is usually summarised by four ideas: **encapsulation** (hide internal state behind an interface), **abstraction** (expose *what* an object does, not *how*), **inheritance** (define a new type by extending an existing one), and **polymorphism** (one interface, many implementations). Those words are easy to recite; the engineering skill is knowing what each one costs. Inheritance in particular is powerful and frequently overused — "favour composition over inheritance" is one of the most repeated pieces of design advice for good reasons.

JavaScript is an unusual OOP language. It has had objects since day one but no classes until ES2015 — instead it uses **prototypes**, where objects inherit directly from other objects. The `class` keyword is largely a cleaner syntax over that prototype machinery. Understanding both layers explains a lot of otherwise surprising behaviour.

This chapter covers objects and classes, encapsulation with `#private` fields, inheritance vs composition, the three kinds of polymorphism, abstraction with TypeScript interfaces and structural typing, prototypes and how `class` maps onto them, and method resolution. It points forward to SOLID (Phase 10), design patterns (Phase 9), and programming paradigms (Phase 13) rather than duplicating them.

sections.caption: The four classic OOP ideas and the JavaScript/TypeScript features that implement them. Inheritance is the pillar most often replaced by composition in modern designs.

sections.title: Blueprints, Houses, and Building Codes
sections.content:
A **class** is an architect's blueprint; an **object** is a house built from it. One blueprint can produce a whole street of houses, each with its own furniture and paint (its own *state*) but the same floor plan and wiring (shared *behaviour*).

**Encapsulation** is the wall around the electrical panel. Residents interact through switches and sockets — a small, safe interface. They cannot reach in and rewire the mains, so the house's invariants ("no circuit exceeds 20 amps") stay true no matter who lives there.

**Abstraction** is the building code's definition of a "socket": a standard shape that delivers power. Any appliance designed for that interface works, whether the house runs on solar or grid power.

**Inheritance** is drawing a "house with garage" blueprint by photocopying the base blueprint and adding a garage. Convenient — until the original architect moves a load-bearing wall and every derived blueprint silently changes with it. **Composition** is the alternative: build the house from standard modules (a kitchen module, a garage module) that plug together. Swap a module and nothing else needs to change.

**Polymorphism** is the light switch: you flip it the same way whether it controls an LED, a fan, or a garage door. One interface, many behaviours behind it.

sections.title: Objects and Classes
sections.content:
An **object** is a bundle of **state** (fields, properties) and **behaviour** (methods) with an **identity**: two objects with identical fields are still two different objects (`{a: 1} !== {a: 1}`). A **class** is a template that describes which fields and methods its instances have, plus a **constructor** that initialises a new instance into a valid state.

In JavaScript you can create objects without any class at all — object literals, `Object.create(proto)`, or factory functions — and that flexibility is used heavily in idiomatic code. Classes add a standard way to define *many* objects of the same kind:

```javascript
class Point {
  x = 0;                     // public instance field
  y = 0;
  static ORIGIN = new Point(); // static field: belongs to the class itself
  constructor(x, y) { this.x = x ?? 0; this.y = y ?? 0; }
  distanceTo(other) { return Math.hypot(this.x - other.x, this.y - other.y); }
}
```

Key vocabulary:

- **Instance members** belong to each object (`p.x`). In JS, fields are created per instance; methods live once on the shared prototype.
- **Static members** belong to the class (`Point.ORIGIN`, `Array.from`), useful for factories and constants.
- **Constructor** — runs once per `new`, should leave the object in a valid state (establish the **class invariant**). If construction can fail, throw rather than returning a half-built object.
- **Accessors** (`get`/`set`) look like fields but run code, so a class can validate writes or compute values lazily.

A useful design lens is **tell, don't ask**: rather than pulling data out of an object and deciding outside (`if (acct.balance >= x) acct.balance -= x`), tell the object what you want (`acct.withdraw(x)`) and let it enforce its rules. Objects that are only bags of getters and setters with all logic elsewhere are sometimes called an **anemic domain model** — they pay OOP's costs without its benefits.

Not every piece of data needs a class. Plain objects and records (`{ id, name }`, TypeScript `type`s) are often better for data that is just passed around, serialised, or transformed. Reach for a class when there is **state plus rules** to protect.

sections.title: Encapsulation: Hiding State Behind an Interface
sections.content:
**Encapsulation** means an object's internal state can only be changed through its methods, so the object can guarantee its invariants ("balance is never negative"). It also lets you change the internal representation later without breaking callers — the interface is the contract; the fields are an implementation detail.

JavaScript has several levels of privacy, and the differences matter:

| Technique | Enforced by | Visible via `Object.keys`/JSON? | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `_balance` naming convention | Nobody | Yes | Just a hint to humans |
| TypeScript `private balance` | Compiler only | Yes | Erased at runtime; `(acct as any).balance` works |
| Closure variables | Language scoping | No | Per-instance functions, no class needed |
| `#balance` (ES2022) | **The JS engine** | No | Hard privacy; access from outside is a *SyntaxError* |

**`#private` fields** are truly private: they are not properties at all, so `obj['#balance']` is `undefined`, they do not appear in `Object.keys`, `JSON.stringify`, or `Proxy` traps, and code outside the class body cannot even mention them. Private methods (`#deposit()`), private static members, and private accessors work the same way. The **ergonomic brand check** `#balance in obj` (ES2022) tests whether an object was constructed by this class — more reliable than `instanceof`, which can be fooled by changing prototypes.

Trade-offs: `#private` members are invisible to subclasses (there is no `protected` in JavaScript; TypeScript's `protected` is compile-time only), and they do not work with `Proxy`-wrapped instances — some libraries that proxy objects (Vue's `reactive()`, some mocking tools) break on them.

Other languages: Java, C#, and C++ have `private`/`protected`/`public` (plus Java's package-private and C#'s `internal`), enforced by the compiler (and, in Java, by the runtime unless reflection is used). Python has no enforced privacy: `_x` is a convention and `__x` triggers name mangling (`_Class__x`), which prevents accidental clashes but not deliberate access. Go uses capitalisation: `Balance` is exported from the package, `balance` is not.

Encapsulation is about **controlling change**, not secrecy — a public method that hands out a mutable internal array (`getItems() { return this.#items; }`) breaks encapsulation as surely as a public field. Return copies or read-only views.

sections.label: Encapsulation
sections.explanation: `#balance`, `#count`, and `#deposit` are engine-enforced private members: they are absent from `Object.keys` and JSON, and `acct['#balance']` is just an unrelated missing property. The `balance` getter exposes a read-only view; assigning to it does nothing in sloppy mode (and throws in strict mode) because there is no setter. All state changes go through `deposit`/`withdraw`, which validate input. `#balance in obj` is a brand check that is true only for objects constructed by this class.

sections.title: Inheritance: Reuse Through "Is-A"
sections.content:
**Inheritance** defines a new class (the subclass, child, or derived class) by extending an existing one (the superclass, parent, or base class). The subclass inherits the parent's fields and methods, can add new ones, and can **override** existing methods. `super(...)` calls the parent constructor; `super.method()` calls the parent's version of an overridden method.

```javascript
class Employee { constructor(name) { this.name = name; } pay() { return 1000; } }
class Manager extends Employee { pay() { return super.pay() + 500; } }
```

In a derived class, `this` does not exist until `super()` returns — touching `this` earlier throws `ReferenceError` — and subclass field initialisers run *after* `super()`.

Inheritance models an **is-a** relationship: a `Manager` *is an* `Employee` and must be usable anywhere an `Employee` is expected. That last requirement is the **Liskov Substitution Principle** (the "L" in SOLID, covered in Phase 10). The textbook violation is `Square extends Rectangle`: setting a square's width must also change its height, which breaks code that assumes width and height are independent.

Languages differ in how much inheritance they allow:

- **Single inheritance** of classes: Java, C#, JavaScript, Swift, Kotlin. Java and C# allow implementing many *interfaces*; Java 8+ interfaces can carry default methods.
- **Multiple inheritance**: C++ and Python. Python resolves conflicts with the **C3 linearisation** method resolution order (`Class.__mro__`); C++ needs `virtual` inheritance to avoid duplicating a shared base in the "diamond".
- **No class inheritance**: Go and Rust deliberately omit it. Go offers struct **embedding** (automatic delegation to an embedded field) and implicit interfaces; Rust uses **traits** with default methods.

The main costs of inheritance:

- **Tight coupling to the parent's implementation.** Subclasses often depend on *how* the parent works internally, not just its public contract — the **fragile base class problem**. A harmless-looking change in the parent can break every child.
- **Rigid taxonomies.** Real domains rarely form a clean tree. "FlyingAnimal" vs "SwimmingAnimal" falls apart at the first duck; deep hierarchies end up with methods that throw "not supported".
- **Inheriting too much.** Joe Armstrong's quip: "You wanted a banana but what you got was a gorilla holding the banana and the entire jungle."

sections.title: Composition Over Inheritance
sections.content:
**Composition** builds an object out of other objects that it *has* and *delegates to* — a **has-a** relationship. A `Car` has an `Engine`; it does not extend one. "Favour object composition over class inheritance" was a central principle of the *Design Patterns* book (Gang of Four, 1994), and Joshua Bloch's *Effective Java* devotes an item to it with the canonical example: a `HashSet` subclass that counts insertions double-counts because the parent's `addAll` internally calls the overridden `add`.

Why composition is usually the better default:

1. **Depends only on the public interface.** A wrapper calls the component's public methods; it does not care how they are implemented, so the component can change freely.
2. **Flexible at runtime.** You can swap the component (a different storage backend, a mock in tests) or choose it per instance. An inheritance relationship is fixed at compile time.
3. **Mix behaviours freely.** A duck can be composed from "can fly", "can swim", and "can quack" capabilities; a penguin takes only "can swim". No awkward overrides that throw.
4. **Smaller surface.** The wrapper exposes only what it chooses, instead of inheriting every parent method (including ones that could break its invariants).

When inheritance is still the right tool: a genuine, stable is-a relationship where substitutability holds; frameworks that are designed for extension (`class MyElement extends HTMLElement` for Web Components, `extends Error` for custom errors); and small, shallow hierarchies (one or two levels) with a parent designed for subclassing. A good heuristic: **inherit interfaces, compose implementations.**

In JavaScript, composition shows up as plain wrapping (a private field holding a collaborator), **dependency injection** (passing collaborators into the constructor), object spreading/`Object.assign` of behaviour objects, and **mixins** — functions that take a class and return a subclass with extra methods (`const Serializable = (Base) => class extends Base { toJSON() {...} }`). Mixins still use inheritance under the hood, so they inherit some of its fragility; prefer plain delegation when it is enough. Many patterns from Phase 9 — Strategy, Decorator, Adapter, Composite — are structured applications of composition.

sections.caption: Inheritance vs composition for the same feature. CountingSet extends Set and is coupled to when Set calls add internally; CountingBag owns a private Set and delegates to it, depending only on its public methods.

sections.label: Inheritance vs composition
sections.explanation: The `Set` constructor adds initial values by calling `this.add()` — which dispatches to the subclass override before the subclass's `added = 0` field initialiser runs. The increments land on a not-yet-initialised field, then the initialiser resets it to 0, so the two constructor elements are never counted. That is the fragile base class problem: the subclass depends on *when and whether* the parent calls its own methods. `CountingBag` wraps a private `Set` instead, controls every code path, and counts all four. The duck/penguin factories compose capabilities rather than forcing them into a single hierarchy.

sections.title: Polymorphism: Subtype, Ad-hoc, and Parametric
sections.content:
**Polymorphism** ("many forms") means one piece of code works with values of different types. Computer science distinguishes three kinds (terminology from Christopher Strachey, 1967, and Cardelli and Wegner, 1985), and interviewers like to ask for all three.

**1. Subtype (inclusion) polymorphism** — what most people mean by "polymorphism" in OOP. Code written against a supertype (`Shape`) works with any subtype (`Circle`, `Rect`), and the *runtime type* of the object decides which method runs: `shape.area()` calls `Circle.prototype.area` or `Rect.prototype.area`. This is **dynamic dispatch** (late binding). It is what lets you replace a chain of `if (type === 'circle') ... else if ...` with a single method call, and add new types without editing existing code (the open/closed principle). In Java, Python, and JavaScript instance methods dispatch dynamically by default; in C++ and C# only methods declared `virtual` do.

**2. Ad-hoc polymorphism** — the same name has *different implementations for different argument types*, chosen per type. Forms include:

- **Function/method overloading** (Java, C#, C++): `print(int)` and `print(String)` are separate methods, chosen at **compile time** from the static argument types.
- **Operator overloading** (C++, Python `__add__`, Kotlin, C#): `a + b` means different things for numbers, strings, and vectors.
- **Type classes/traits** (Haskell, Rust): a type opts in by implementing an interface for itself.

JavaScript has **no real overloading**: a second function with the same name replaces the first. You emulate it by checking argument types at runtime. TypeScript adds **overload signatures**, which give callers precise types for each call form, backed by a *single* implementation that must branch on the arguments.

**3. Parametric polymorphism (generics)** — code written once for *any* type `T`, with identical behaviour for all of them: `Stack<T>`, `Array<T>`, `Map<K, V>`, `Promise<T>`. **Bounded** generics (`<T extends Shape>`) require `T` to have certain members. Implementations differ: Java uses **type erasure** (one compiled class, generic types checked then removed); C++ templates and Rust generics are **monomorphised** (a specialised copy per type, fast but larger binaries); Go has had generics since 1.18 (2022); TypeScript generics are erased entirely, since JS has no runtime types.

**Duck typing** is the dynamic-language flavour of polymorphism: "if it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it is a duck". JavaScript and Python simply call the method and succeed if it exists. TypeScript's structural typing is the statically checked version of the same idea.

sections.title: Abstraction, Interfaces, and Structural Typing
sections.content:
**Abstraction** means exposing *what* something does while hiding *how*. A caller of `storage.save(doc)` should not need to know whether it writes to disk, S3, or memory. Abstraction is what makes large systems understandable: each layer lets you forget the details below it.

Two tools express abstractions in typed OOP:

- An **interface** declares a contract — method signatures and properties — with no implementation. Anything that satisfies it can be used.
- An **abstract class** can mix implemented methods with **abstract** ones that subclasses must provide. It cannot be instantiated directly. It is useful when implementations share real code, as in the **template method** pattern: `describe()` is written once in the base class and calls the abstract `area()` hook.

Prefer interfaces for contracts between modules; use abstract classes when there is genuinely shared implementation, and keep them shallow.

**TypeScript interfaces are structural.** A value satisfies an interface if it has the required members with compatible types — no `implements` declaration needed. An object literal `{ name: 'triangle', area: () => 6 }` is a valid `Shape`. The `implements` clause on a class is only an extra compile-time check. This contrasts with **nominal typing** in Java, C#, Swift, and Rust, where a type must *explicitly declare* that it implements an interface or trait; two identically shaped types with different names are not interchangeable. Go sits in between: its interfaces are statically checked but satisfied **implicitly**, like TypeScript.

Consequences of structural typing worth knowing:

- Great for testing and integration: any object with the right shape can stand in, no inheritance required.
- **Accidental compatibility**: `UserId` and `OrderId` that are both `string` are interchangeable. Teams use **branded types** (`string & { __brand: 'UserId' }`) to simulate nominal typing.
- **Erasure**: TypeScript interfaces, generics, and `abstract`/`private` modifiers vanish at runtime. You cannot `instanceof` an interface; runtime checks need type guards, `#private` brand checks, or schema validators (Zod, Valibot).
- Excess-property checks apply only to fresh object literals, which surprises people who expect strict shape matching everywhere.

Since Node.js 23.6, `node file.ts` runs TypeScript directly by **stripping types** (enabled by default in Node 22.18+ as well). It supports erasable syntax only — interfaces, generics, `abstract`, type annotations — but not `enum`s, `namespace`s, or constructor parameter properties (`constructor(private x: number)`), which generate JavaScript code. The example below sticks to erasable syntax.

sections.label: Polymorphism & interfaces (TypeScript)
sections.explanation: `describe()` is written once in `BaseShape` and calls the abstract `area()`; dynamic dispatch selects `Circle` or `Rect` at runtime (subtype polymorphism). The plain `triangle` object never mentions `Shape` but is accepted by `totalArea` because TypeScript checks structure, not names. `format` has two overload signatures backed by one implementation that branches on the runtime type (ad-hoc polymorphism). `Stack<T>` and `largest<T extends Shape>` are parametric polymorphism; all the types are erased when Node runs the file. The output matches the comments with `node c3.ts` on Node 23.6+ (or `npx tsx`).

sections.title: Prototypes: How JavaScript Really Does Objects
sections.content:
Most class-based languages copy a class's structure into each instance and look methods up in a per-class table. JavaScript instead uses **prototypal inheritance**: every object has an internal link, `[[Prototype]]`, to another object (or `null`). When you read a property that the object does not have, the engine follows that link and looks there, then that object's prototype, and so on — the **prototype chain** — until it finds the property or reaches `null` (result: `undefined`).

You can inspect and set the link with `Object.getPrototypeOf(obj)` and `Object.setPrototypeOf(obj, proto)`, or create an object with a chosen prototype via `Object.create(proto)`. (The `__proto__` accessor still works but is legacy.)

Every regular function has a `prototype` property — an object that becomes the `[[Prototype]]` of instances created with `new`. `new Fn(args)` does four things:

1. Creates a new empty object.
2. Sets its `[[Prototype]]` to `Fn.prototype`.
3. Calls `Fn` with `this` bound to the new object.
4. Returns the new object (unless `Fn` explicitly returns another object).

A `class` declaration builds exactly this structure: the class *is* a constructor function, methods are placed on `ClassName.prototype`, and `extends` links `Child.prototype` to `Parent.prototype` (for instances) and `Child` to `Parent` (so static methods are inherited too). That is why people call `class` "syntactic sugar".

It is *mostly* sugar — classes also add behaviour the old pattern lacked: calling a class without `new` throws `TypeError`; class bodies are always strict mode; methods are **non-enumerable**; `super` works via a hidden `[[HomeObject]]`; subclasses of built-ins like `Array`, `Error`, and `Map` work correctly; and `#private` fields and `static` blocks have no prototype-era equivalent.

Practical consequences of the prototype model:

- **Methods are shared.** All instances point to one function on the prototype — memory-efficient. Arrow-function class fields (`handle = () => {}`) are the exception: one copy per instance.
- **Prototypes are live.** Adding a method to `Animal.prototype` instantly gives it to every existing animal. That is also why **monkey-patching built-ins** (`Array.prototype.myThing`) is dangerous: it affects all code on the page and can collide with future standard methods (this is why the standard `Array.prototype.flatten` had to be renamed `flat`).
- **Own vs inherited properties.** `Object.hasOwn(obj, key)` checks only the object itself; `key in obj` and `for...in` include the chain.

sections.label: class vs prototypes
sections.explanation: `Dog`/`Animal` and `DogFn`/`AnimalFn` produce the same structure: a constructor call for `super(name)`, two `setPrototypeOf` calls for `extends`, and an explicit parent call for `super.speak()`. `typeof Dog` is `'function'`, and the loop walks the exact chain from the diagram. An own property shadows the prototype's `speak`, methods are shared across instances, and patching `Animal.prototype` affects existing instances. The last lines show what makes `class` more than sugar: it refuses calls without `new`, and its methods are non-enumerable.

sections.title: Method Resolution and Dynamic Dispatch
sections.content:
**Method resolution** answers: when code calls `obj.speak()`, which function runs? In JavaScript the algorithm is the prototype-chain lookup: check `obj`'s own properties, then each prototype in order; the **first** match wins. Then the function is called with `this = obj` — the *original* receiver, not the prototype where the method was found. That is why an inherited method can read the instance's fields, and why a parent method that calls `this.add()` reaches the subclass override (the mechanism behind both polymorphism and the fragile base class problem).

`super.method()` is different: it starts the lookup at the prototype of the object where the *current method was defined* (its `[[HomeObject]]`), not at `this`. So `super` is resolved lexically, while `this.method()` is resolved dynamically.

How other runtimes resolve methods:

- **Java, C#, C++ (virtual)**: each class has a **vtable**, an array of method pointers. Each object carries a pointer to its class's vtable, and a call is an indexed jump — constant time. Interface calls use itables or similar structures. Non-virtual C++ methods, `static`, `final`, and `private` methods can be bound at compile time.
- **Python**: looks up the attribute on the instance, then along the class's **MRO** (Method Resolution Order, computed with C3 linearisation to handle multiple inheritance consistently).
- **Smalltalk/Objective-C/Ruby**: "message sending" — look up the selector at runtime, with per-class method caches and a fallback hook (`doesNotUnderstand:`, `method_missing`) when lookup fails.

A naive prototype-chain walk on every call would be slow, so V8 and other engines optimise heavily. Each object has a **hidden class** (V8 calls it a *Map*) describing its layout; call sites keep **inline caches** that remember "for objects with this hidden class, `speak` is at this location". Calls on objects of one shape (**monomorphic**) are nearly as fast as a vtable jump; sites that see many shapes (**megamorphic**) fall back to slower lookups. Practical tips that follow: initialise all fields in the constructor (or as class fields) in a consistent order, avoid `delete obj.prop` on hot objects, and avoid changing an object's prototype after creation (`setPrototypeOf` on live objects deoptimises code that touched them).

sections.title: OOP in Context: SOLID, Patterns, and Other Paradigms
sections.content:
This chapter covers the mechanics. Three later phases build on them; here is where each fits so you know what *not* to look for here.

**SOLID (Phase 10).** Five design principles for object-oriented code — Single responsibility, Open/closed, Liskov substitution, Interface segregation, Dependency inversion. You have already met two of them implicitly: substitutability is what makes subtype polymorphism safe, and depending on interfaces instead of concrete classes is what makes composition flexible.

**Design patterns (Phase 9).** Named, reusable solutions built from OOP mechanics — Strategy, Observer, Decorator, Factory, Adapter, and others. Most are applications of "program to an interface" plus composition.

**Paradigms (Phase 13).** OOP is one way to structure code among several:

- **Procedural** code keeps data and functions separate; simple and direct for scripts and low-level code.
- **Functional** programming favours immutable data and pure functions; behaviour is composed from functions instead of bundled into objects. Where OOP makes it easy to add new *types* (a new `Shape` subclass), functional code with pattern matching makes it easy to add new *operations* — the two sides of the **expression problem**.
- **Data-oriented** design organises data by access pattern (arrays of fields instead of arrays of objects) for cache efficiency in games and high-performance systems.

Modern languages are **multi-paradigm**. Idiomatic TypeScript mixes classes for stateful components with plain objects, closures, and pure functions for data transformation; Rust and Go provide interfaces/traits and methods without class inheritance; Kotlin, Swift, and Scala blend OOP with functional features. The practical takeaway: use objects where you have **state with invariants** and multiple interchangeable **implementations behind an interface**; use plain data and functions where you are mostly transforming values.

**Common mistakes**

- **Inheriting for code reuse** when there is no true is-a relationship. If a subclass overrides methods to throw "not supported", the hierarchy is wrong — compose instead.
- **Deep hierarchies** (more than two or three levels). Each level couples to every level above it.
- **Calling overridable methods from a constructor.** The subclass override runs before the subclass's fields are initialised (the `CountingSet` bug).
- **Assuming TypeScript `private` is runtime privacy.** It is erased; use `#private` when it must be enforced.
- **Getter/setter for every field** — that is a public field with extra steps. Expose behaviour, not state.
- **Leaking internal mutable state** by returning internal arrays or objects directly.
- **Monkey-patching built-in prototypes** in application or library code.
- **Using arrow-function class fields everywhere** "just in case" — one function copy per instance and they cannot be overridden via `super`. Use them for callbacks that need bound `this`.
- **Using `instanceof` across realms** (iframes, multiple package copies) — it compares prototype identity and fails; prefer brand checks or duck typing.

**Interview angles.** Be ready to: (1) name the four pillars *and* say what each costs; (2) define the three kinds of polymorphism with one example each (`shape.area()`, overloading/operator `+`, `List<T>`); (3) explain why composition is usually preferred, using the fragile base class problem; (4) explain that JS `class` creates a constructor function plus a prototype chain, and what `new` does in four steps; (5) contrast structural (TypeScript, Go) with nominal (Java, C#) typing; (6) explain dynamic dispatch — vtables in Java/C++, prototype lookup plus inline caches in JS.

items: An **object** bundles state with the behaviour that guards it and has its own identity; a **class** is a template with a constructor that establishes a valid initial state. Use classes when there is state plus rules to protect; plain objects suffice for passive data.

**Encapsulation** controls change: state is modified only through methods that enforce invariants. In JS, `#private` fields (ES2022) are engine-enforced and invisible to `Object.keys`/JSON; TypeScript `private` is compile-time only; `_name` is just a convention. `#field in obj` is a reliable brand check.

**Inheritance** models is-a and must respect Liskov substitution. Its costs are tight coupling to the parent's implementation (the **fragile base class** problem), rigid taxonomies, and inheriting unwanted members. JS, Java, and C# allow single class inheritance; C++ and Python allow multiple; Go and Rust have none.

**Favour composition over inheritance**: has-a relationships depend only on public interfaces, can be swapped at runtime, and let you mix behaviours freely. Inherit interfaces, compose implementations; keep any hierarchy shallow.

**Polymorphism** comes in three kinds: **subtype** (dynamic dispatch on the runtime type, e.g. `shape.area()`), **ad-hoc** (overloading and operator overloading, chosen per argument type; JS has none natively, TS has overload signatures), and **parametric** (generics such as `Stack<T>`, optionally bounded with `T extends Shape`).

**Abstraction** exposes what, hides how. Interfaces declare contracts; abstract classes add shared implementation (template method). **TypeScript is structurally typed** — any value with the right shape satisfies an interface — while Java and C# are nominal. All TS types are erased at runtime.

JavaScript objects inherit through the **prototype chain**: property lookup walks `[[Prototype]]` links until a match or `null`. `class` builds a constructor function with methods on `.prototype` and `extends` links the prototypes, but adds real differences: requires `new`, strict mode, non-enumerable methods, `super`, and `#private`.

`new Fn()` creates an object, links it to `Fn.prototype`, runs `Fn` with `this` bound to it, and returns it. Methods on the prototype are shared by all instances and patches to a prototype affect existing objects.

**Method resolution**: JS uses first-match prototype lookup with `this` bound to the original receiver, while `super` starts above the method's home object. Java/C++ use vtables, Python uses the C3 MRO. V8 speeds lookups with hidden classes and inline caches, so keep object shapes consistent.

OOP is one paradigm among several. SOLID (Phase 10) and design patterns (Phase 9) build on these mechanics; functional and procedural styles (Phase 13) are often better for pure data transformation. Modern TypeScript is multi-paradigm.

quiz.question: What is the main purpose of encapsulation?
options: To make objects load faster by hiding unused fields
To ensure state changes only through methods that can enforce invariants, so internals can change without breaking callers
To allow subclasses to access all of the parent's fields
To encrypt sensitive data held in memory
quiz.explanation: Encapsulation is about controlling change: the object owns its state and exposes an interface that preserves its invariants. It is not a performance or security (encryption) feature, and it restricts rather than widens access.

quiz.question: How does a TypeScript `private balance` field differ from a JavaScript `#balance` field?
options: They are identical after compilation
`#balance` is checked only by the compiler, `private` is enforced at runtime
`private` is checked only at compile time and erased, while `#balance` is enforced by the JavaScript engine at runtime
`private` fields cannot be read by methods of the same class
quiz.explanation: TypeScript access modifiers vanish when types are erased; `(obj as any).balance` works at runtime and the field appears in JSON. `#private` fields are not properties at all and cannot be accessed from outside the class body.

quiz.question: A subclass of `Set` overrides `add()` to count insertions and initialises `count = 0` as a class field. Elements passed to the constructor are not counted. Why?
options: The Set constructor calls the overridden add() before the subclass field initialiser runs, and the initialiser then resets count to 0
Set ignores overridden methods when called from its constructor
Class fields are shared between all instances
super() must be called after field initialisers
quiz.explanation: During super(), Set calls this.add(), which dispatches to the subclass override. Subclass fields are initialised only after super() returns, so count is reset to 0. This is the fragile base class problem: the subclass depends on the parent's internal call pattern.

quiz.question: Which is the strongest reason to prefer composition over inheritance?
options: Composition always uses less memory
Inheritance is not supported in TypeScript
Composed objects cannot have methods
A wrapper depends only on its component's public interface, so implementations can change or be swapped without breaking it
quiz.explanation: Composition couples to a public contract instead of the parent's implementation details, and the component can be replaced at runtime or in tests. Memory use is not the reason, and TypeScript supports inheritance.

quiz.question: Java's `print(int)` and `print(String)` methods, selected by argument type at compile time, are an example of which kind of polymorphism?
options: Parametric polymorphism
Subtype polymorphism
Ad-hoc polymorphism
Duck typing
quiz.explanation: Overloading provides different implementations of one name for different argument types — ad-hoc polymorphism. Parametric polymorphism is one implementation for all types (generics); subtype polymorphism dispatches on the receiver's runtime type.

quiz.question: In TypeScript, an object literal `{ name: "t", area: () => 6 }` is passed where a `Shape` interface (`name: string; area(): number`) is expected. What happens?
options: It type-checks, because TypeScript uses structural typing
It fails, because the object does not declare `implements Shape`
It fails at runtime with a TypeError
It type-checks only if Shape is an abstract class
quiz.explanation: TypeScript compares shapes, not names: any value with compatible members satisfies the interface. Nominal languages like Java require an explicit implements declaration. Interfaces do not exist at runtime, so there is no runtime check either.

quiz.question: Which of these does `new Dog("Rex")` NOT do, for `class Dog extends Animal`?
options: Create a new object whose [[Prototype]] is Dog.prototype
Run the constructor chain so that this is the new object
Return the new object
Copy all of Dog.prototype's methods onto the new object as own properties
quiz.explanation: Methods stay on the prototype and are found by prototype-chain lookup; they are shared, not copied. `Object.hasOwn(rex, "speak")` is false.

quiz.question: Which statement about JavaScript `class` is FALSE?
options: `typeof` a class returns "function"
A class can be called without `new`, just like a regular function
Class methods are non-enumerable
Class bodies always run in strict mode
quiz.explanation: Calling a class without `new` throws TypeError. That is one of the ways `class` differs from a plain constructor function, along with non-enumerable methods, strict mode, `super`, and `#private` fields.

quiz.question: `Animal.prototype.speak` uses `this.name`. When `rex.speak()` finds `speak` on `Animal.prototype` two levels up the chain, what is `this`?
options: Animal.prototype
Dog.prototype
rex
undefined
quiz.explanation: Lookup finds the function on the prototype, but the call binds `this` to the original receiver `rex`. That is how inherited methods access instance data and how parent methods reach subclass overrides.

quiz.question: A `Square extends Rectangle` class makes `setWidth` also change the height. Code that sets width 5 and height 4 on a Rectangle expects area 20 but gets 16 for a Square. Which principle is violated?
options: Encapsulation
Parametric polymorphism
The open/closed principle
The Liskov Substitution Principle
quiz.explanation: A subtype must be usable anywhere its supertype is expected without breaking correct code. Square changes Rectangle's behavioural contract (independent width and height), so substituting it breaks callers — a Liskov violation, a sign the is-a relationship is wrong.
